questions.question: What effect did reforms have on India's GDP growth rate?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Increased significantly**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The implementation of the **New Economic Policy (NEP)** in **1991** marked a decisive shift from a state-controlled, inward-looking economy to a liberalized, market-oriented system.
 
• Prior to these reforms, the Indian economy was characterized by the **Hindu Rate of Growth**, which stagnated around **3.5% to 4%** from the 1950s through the 1980s.
 
• Post-reform data demonstrates that the **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** growth rate surged, averaging nearly **6.5%** in the 1990s and climbing to peaks of **8% to 9%** during the mid-2000s.
 
• The abolition of the **License-Permit Raj** removed industrial bottlenecks, allowing private enterprises to expand rapidly and enhancing overall economic productivity.
 
• Increased **Global Integration** and the reduction of trade barriers allowed India to transition from a sluggish agrarian-focused economy to one of the **fastest-growing major economies** in the world.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Balance of Payments (BoP) Crisis**:

 
 
• The reforms were necessitated by a severe crisis in **1991** where foreign exchange reserves fell to approximately **$1.2 billion**, barely enough for two weeks of essential imports.
 
 
 
• **Architects of Reform**:
 
 
• The policy shift was spearheaded by the then Prime Minister **P. V. Narasimha Rao** and Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh** under the guidance of the **IMF** and **World Bank**.
 
 
 
• **Sectoral Growth**:
 
 
• **Service Sector**: Post-1991, this sector became the primary engine of growth, specifically in **Information Technology (IT)** and **Telecommunications**, now contributing over **50%** to India's GDP.
 
• **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**: Reforms opened various sectors to foreign capital, leading to a massive influx of investment and modern technology.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Policy 1991**:
 
 
• This policy drastically reduced the number of industries reserved for the **Public Sector** and introduced **Disinvestment** to improve the efficiency of **PSUs**.

questions.question: The term 'Kriti' in Carnatic music refers to:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**a compositional lyric form**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **Kriti** refers to the most highly evolved and predominant **compositional lyric form** in **Carnatic classical music**, forming the backbone of modern concert repertoires.
 
• A standard **Kriti** follows a tripartite structural arrangement consisting of the **Pallavi** (the thematic opening), the **Anupallavi** (the second section), and the **Charanam** (the final stanzas that conclude the piece).
 
• The evolution of the **Kriti** is credited largely to the **Trinity of Carnatic Music**—**Tyagaraja**, **Muthuswami Dikshitar**, and **Syama Sastri**—who refined the form in the late **18th and early 19th centuries**.
 
• Unlike simpler devotional songs, a **Kriti** emphasizes **musical technicality** and **raga bhava** (the essence of the melody), where the **Sahitya** (lyrics) serves as a vehicle for complex melodic exploration.
 
• It is characterized by its fixed nature, where the **Dhatu** (musical setting) and **Matu** (lyrical content) are pre-composed, although performers often add improvisational elements like **Niraval** or **Kalpanaswaras** during its rendition.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Raga**

 
 
• Defined as a **melodic scale** or framework that provides the basis for composition and improvisation in Indian music.
 
• It uses a specific set of notes (**Swaras**) and rules of ascent (**Arohana**) and descent (**Avarohana**).
 
 
 
• **Tala**
 
 
• Refers to the **rhythmic pattern** or time cycle that regulates the temporal aspect of a musical performance.
 
• Common examples include **Adi Tala** (8 beats) and **Rupaka Tala** (3 beats).
 
 
 
• **Gamaka**
 
 
• Represents a **type of musical ornamentation** involving the graceful manipulation of notes to provide aesthetic depth.
 
• It is a vital component that distinguishes the unique character of different **Ragas**.
 
 
 
• **Varnam**
 
 
• A foundational **compositional form** usually performed at the beginning of a concert to showcase the characteristic phrases of a **Raga**.

questions.question: The peeling of curved sheets from massive rocks due to temperature changes is known as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Exfoliation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Exfoliation** is a type of **mechanical weathering** or physical weathering process where the external layers of a rock peel away in thin, **curved sheets** or shells.
 
• This process is often referred to as **onion-skin weathering** because the rock flakes off in layers, similar to an onion.
 
• It is primarily caused by **thermal expansion** and contraction. Rocks are poor conductors of heat; therefore, intense solar heating during the day causes the **outer layer** to expand more than the interior. Cooling at night causes contraction, leading to **differential stresses** that fracture the rock parallel to the surface.
 
• **Pressure release**, also known as **unloading**, is another significant cause. When heavy overlying rock or ice is removed by **erosion**, the underlying **massive rocks** (such as **granite**) expand outward, creating joints that result in the peeling of large curved slabs.
 
• This phenomenon is most prevalent in **arid** and **semi-arid** environments where there are large **diurnal temperature ranges**, and in mountainous regions with high rates of **denudation**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Carbonation**

 
 
• A **chemical weathering** process where **carbon dioxide** from the atmosphere dissolves in rainwater to form weak **carbonic acid**.
 
• It reacts specifically with **carbonate minerals** like **calcite** found in **limestone** and **marble**, leading to the formation of **calcium bicarbonate** which is easily washed away.
 
 
 
• **Salt Crystallisation**
 
 
• A form of **physical weathering** common in coastal or **desert** regions.
 
• Saline water enters **pore spaces** or joints in rocks; upon evaporation, **salt crystals** grow and exert **expansive force**, eventually disintegrating the rock structure.
 
 
 
• **Abrasion**
 
 
• The **mechanical scraping** or wearing down of rock surfaces through **friction**.
 
• It is caused by the **scouring action** of particles (sand, pebbles) transported by **wind**, **glaciers**, or **river currents** hitting against stationary rock bodies.

questions.question: Which of the following sectors includes activities like trade, transport, and communication in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tertiary**__.

__
 
• The **Tertiary sector** is popularly known as the **Service sector** because it involves providing services to both consumers and businesses rather than producing physical goods.
 
• Activities in this sector, such as **Transport**, **Trade**, **Storage**, and **Communication**, act as a support system for the development of the **Primary** and **Secondary** sectors.
 
• In the Indian economy, the **Tertiary sector** has emerged as the largest contributing sector to the **Gross Value Added (GVA)**, surpassing the industrial and agricultural sectors in recent decades.
 
• Other vital services included in this category are **Banking**, **Insurance**, **Tourism**, **Education**, and **Healthcare**, which are essential for a modern economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Primary Sector**:

 
 
• Involves the direct extraction and use of **natural resources** from the earth.
 
• Key examples include **Agriculture**, **Fishing**, **Mining**, **Forestry**, and **Dairy farming**.
 
• It serves as the raw material base for all other economic activities.
 
 
 
• **Secondary Sector**:
 
 
• Focuses on the **manufacturing** and processing of raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods.
 
• Commonly referred to as the **Industrial Sector**, it includes **Construction**, **Manufacturing**, and **Electricity generation**.
 
• Examples include converting **Sugarcane into Sugar** or **Cotton into Textiles**.

• Representing the highest level of decision-making, it is a specialized sub-division of the service economy.
 
• It includes **Top Government Officials**, **Senior Business Executives**, and **Research Scientists** who focus on the creation and interpretation of new ideas.

questions.question: The Twenty-Ninth Amendment Act of 1972 included which of the following in the Ninth Schedule?

options.text: Two Kerala Acts on land reforms

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Two Kerala Acts on land reforms**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Twenty-Ninth Amendment Act, 1972** was specifically enacted to provide constitutional protection to certain land reform legislations passed by the **Kerala State Legislature**.
 
• The amendment included two specific acts in the **Ninth Schedule** of the Constitution: the **Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969** (Act 35 of 1969) and the **Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1971** (Act 25 of 1971).
 
• By placing these acts in the **Ninth Schedule**, the government aimed to shield them from judicial scrutiny under **Article 31B**, preventing them from being declared void on the grounds of violating **Fundamental Rights**, particularly the then-existing right to property.
 
• The validity of this amendment, along with the **24th and 25th Amendments**, was later challenged in the landmark **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)** case, which is famous for establishing the **Basic Structure Doctrine** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The amendment was a response to the litigation faced by the state government while implementing radical land redistribution policies intended to abolish the intermediary system and set ceilings on land holdings.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ninth Schedule**:

 
 
• It was introduced by the **First Amendment Act, 1951** to protect agrarian reform laws from being challenged in courts.
 
• While it initially offered absolute immunity, the Supreme Court in the **I.R. Coelho case (2007)** ruled that laws added after **April 24, 1973**, can be tested against the **Basic Structure**.
 
 
 
• **Reservation in promotions**:
 
 
• This concept is primarily associated with the **77th Amendment Act, 1995**, which inserted clause (4A) into **Article 16**, and the **85th Amendment Act, 2001**, concerning consequential seniority.
 
 
 
• **Special provisions for Mizoram**:
 
 
• Provisions for **Mizoram** were incorporated into the Constitution via the **53rd Amendment Act, 1986**, which added **Article 371G** to protect the religious and social practices of the Mizo people.
 
 
 
• **Environmental protection laws**:
 
 
• These were majorly emphasized during the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, which introduced **Article 48A** in the Directive Principles and **Article 51A(g)** in the Fundamental Duties.

questions.question: What prompted the Kol uprising in the Chhotanagpur region during 1831–32?

options.text: Transfer of tribal lands and intrusion of moneylenders and merchants.
Ban on local festivals perceived as a threat to public order.
Conscription of young men into British units for foreign service.
The spread of famines caused by failures in rice-growing regions.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Transfer of tribal lands and intrusion of moneylenders and merchants.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Kol uprising** of **1831-32** was a significant tribal revolt in the **Chhotanagpur** region against the exploitative policies of the **British East India Company** and their agents.
 
• The primary catalyst was the large-scale **transfer of tribal lands** to outsiders, such as **Sikhs** and **Muslims**, who were granted farming rights by the local **Raja of Chhotanagpur**.
 
• Traditional tribal headmen, known as **Mankis** and **Mundas**, were displaced from their ancestral authority, leading to widespread resentment among the **Munda**, **Oraon**, and **Ho** tribes.
 
• The intrusion of **Dikus** (outsiders), including **moneylenders** and **merchants**, led to extreme economic exploitation through high-interest rates, land alienation, and the introduction of **bonded labor**.
 
• The rebellion was characterized by the burning of houses belonging to outsiders and the destruction of government property, spearheaded by leaders like **Buddhu Bhagat**, who fell in battle in **1832**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Geographical and Social Context**

 
 
• The **Chhotanagpur** plateau covers parts of modern-day **Jharkhand**, **Odisha**, and **Chhattisgarh**, inhabited by diverse tribal groups with unique socio-legal systems.
 
• The **Permanent Settlement** of **1793** indirectly pressured local rulers to maximize revenue, forcing them to lease tribal lands to non-tribal contractors.
 
• The **Kol** tribesmen utilized traditional weapons like bows, arrows, and spears to resist the **British** military units deployed to suppress the movement.
 
• Following the suppression of the revolt, the **British** administration recognized the need for special laws, eventually leading to the creation of the **South-West Frontier Agency** to govern the region more sensitively.

questions.question: The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) visited Kashmir during the reign of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Durlabhavardhana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Xuanzang** (Hiuen Tsang), the celebrated Chinese Buddhist monk and traveler, visited the valley of **Kashmir** in **631 AD** and remained there until **633 AD**.
 
• During this period, **Kashmir** was under the rule of **Durlabhavardhana**, who was the founder of the powerful **Karkota Dynasty**.
 
• The king accorded **Xuanzang** a magnificent royal reception, sending his own maternal uncle to the frontier to escort the pilgrim to the capital city, **Pravarapura** (modern-day **Srinagar**).
 
• **Xuanzang** spent two years in the region studying **Buddhist Sutras** and **Shastras** at the **Jayendra Monastery**, where the king provided him with **twenty scribes** to assist in copying sacred manuscripts.
 
• In his travelogue, **Si-Yu-Ki**, **Xuanzang** praised the king's administration and noted that the kingdom of **Kashmir** held political sway over several adjacent regions, including **Taxila**, **Punch**, and **Rajauri**.
 
• His accounts highlight that **Kashmir** was a major center for the **Sarvastivada** school of Buddhism, housing over **100 monasteries** and **5,000 monks** during the **7th century**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Harshavardhana**:

 
 
• He was the **Pushyabhuti** emperor of **Kannauj** and a contemporary of **Durlabhavardhana**.
 
• While he was **Xuanzang's** primary patron in India and organized the **Prayag Assembly**, he did not rule **Kashmir**, though he reportedly forced the Kashmiri king to surrender a **tooth relic of the Buddha**.
 
 
 
• **Pulakeshin II**:
 
 
• The most renowned king of the **Chalukya Dynasty** of **Badami**.
 
• He is famous for defeating **Harshavardhana** on the banks of the **Narmada River**, but his authority was centered in the **Deccan**, far from **Kashmir**.
 
 
 
• **Yashodharman**:
 
 
• A powerful king of **Malwa** who belonged to the **Aulikara Dynasty**.
 
• He achieved historical fame for defeating the **Huna** ruler **Mihirakula** in the **6th century**, which was nearly a century before **Xuanzang** arrived in India.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs is formed inside limestone caves by deposition?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Stalactites and stalagmites**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Stalactites** and **stalagmites** are the most common **depositional landforms** found within **limestone caves**, which are characteristic features of **Karst topography**.
 
• **Stalactites** are icicle-like structures that hang from the **cave ceiling**; they form when mineral-rich water drips through cracks in the rock, leaving behind tiny deposits of **calcium carbonate** (calcite) as **carbon dioxide** escapes into the cave air.
 
• **Stalagmites** are mounds or pillars that grow upward from the **cave floor**, created by the accumulation of **calcite** deposited by water dripping from the ceiling or the tips of stalactites above.
 
• The formation process relies on **carbonation**, where rainwater mixes with soil **carbon dioxide** to form a weak **carbonic acid** that dissolves the **limestone** (calcium carbonate) into **calcium bicarbonate**; upon entering the cave, the solution undergoes **precipitation** to revert to solid mineral form.
 
• When a stalactite and stalagmite eventually meet, they fuse together to form a continuous vertical **column** or **pillar**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Glacial Landforms**:

 
 
• **Drumlins and eskers**: These are **glacial depositional** features. **Drumlins** are smooth, oval hills of **glacial till**, while **eskers** are long, winding ridges composed of sand and gravel deposited by meltwater streams flowing within or under a glacier.
 
• **Cirques and horns**: These are **glacial erosional** landforms. A **cirque** is a bowl-shaped hollow carved at the head of a glacial valley, and a **horn** is a sharp, pyramid-like mountain peak.
 
 
 
• **Fluvial Landforms**:
 
 
• **Levees and meanders**: These are features of **river systems**. **Meanders** are broad loops or curves in a river's course, and **levees** are natural ridges of **alluvium** (sediment) deposited along the riverbanks during repeated flood events.

• Based on the **Metal Reactivity Series**, **Iron** is more reactive than **Copper**. Consequently, iron has a higher tendency to lose electrons (undergo **oxidation**) compared to copper, allowing it to displace copper ions from the sulphate solution.
 
• The **reddish-brown deposit** formed on the surface of the iron nails is identified as **metallic copper**. This physical change confirms that copper ions (Cu²⁺) have been reduced to solid copper (Cu).

• Because **Iron** is higher than **Copper** in this series, the displacement is spontaneous. However, if a copper nail were placed in an iron sulphate solution, no reaction would occur.

questions.question: The process by which water moves from the soil (high water concentration) into root cells (low water concentration) through a semi-permeable membrane is called ____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Osmosis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Osmosis** is a specific type of **passive transport** where solvent molecules, primarily **water**, move through a **semi-permeable membrane** from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration.
 
• In the soil-root system, the soil environment typically maintains a **high water potential** (low solute concentration), while the **cytoplasm** of the **root hair cells** has a **low water potential** due to the presence of dissolved sugars and salts.
 
• The **plasma membrane** of the plant cell serves as the **selectively permeable barrier**, allowing small water molecules to pass through while blocking the free passage of larger molecules or specific ions.
 
• This movement occurs spontaneously along the **osmotic gradient** and does not require the expenditure of metabolic energy (**ATP**), making it a crucial mechanism for maintaining **turgor pressure** in plant cells.
 
• The absorption of water via this method is the primary way terrestrial plants acquire the moisture necessary for **photosynthesis** and **transpiration**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Diffusion**:

 
 
• It is the general movement of particles (atoms, ions, or molecules) from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
 
• Unlike **osmosis**, it does not require a **membrane** and applies to gases and solutes as well as solvents.
 
 
 
• **Active Transport**:
 
 
• This process involves moving substances, such as **mineral ions**, across a cell membrane against a **concentration gradient**.
 
• It requires **cellular energy** and specific **carrier proteins** to function, allowing roots to accumulate nutrients even when soil concentrations are low.
 
 
 
• **Plasmolysis**:
 
 
• This is the shrinkage of the **protoplast** away from the **cell wall** due to the loss of water.
 
• It occurs when a plant cell is placed in a **hypertonic solution**, leading to water exiting the cell through **exosmosis**.

questions.question: Which of the following tunnels has been inaugurated in January 2026 to improve year-round connectivity between Sonamarg and Srinagar?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Z-Morh tunnel**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Z-Morh tunnel** is a strategic **6.5 km long** road tunnel located in the **Ganderbal district** of **Jammu and Kashmir**, designed to provide **all-weather connectivity** between **Srinagar** and **Sonamarg**.
 
• The tunnel is constructed on the **Srinagar-Leh Highway (NH-1)** and was officially inaugurated in **January 2026** to bypass the treacherous **Z-Morh** (Z-curve) stretch, which remains closed during winters due to heavy **snowfall** and **avalanches**.
 
• Situated at an altitude of approximately **2,637 meters**, it ensures that the tourist destination of **Sonamarg** remains accessible throughout the year, boosting the local **economy** and **tourism** sector.
 
• The project includes a **main tunnel** and a **parallel escape tunnel**, featuring advanced **Integrated Fire Control** systems, **automated ventilation**, and **CCTV monitoring** for passenger safety.
 
• Strategically, the tunnel serves as a vital precursor to the **Zojila Tunnel**, facilitating smoother movement for **defense forces** and **logistics** towards the **Ladakh** region regardless of weather conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Atal Tunnel**:

 
 
• Located in **Himachal Pradesh**, it spans **9.02 km** and connects **Manali** to the **Lahaul-Spiti valley**.
 
• It is the world's longest **highway tunnel** above an altitude of **10,000 feet** and was inaugurated in **October 2020**.
 
 
 
• **Pir Panjal Tunnel**:
 
 
• This refers to the **11.2 km** long **railway tunnel** on the **Banihal-Qazigund** section of the **USBRL project**.
 
• It pierces through the **Pir Panjal Range** and is currently the longest **transportation railway tunnel** in India.
 
 
 
• **Nehru Tunnel (Jawahar Tunnel)**:
 
 
• Constructed in the **1950s**, this **2.85 km** tunnel connects **Banihal** and **Qazigund** across the **Banihal Pass**.
 
• It was the primary **all-weather link** between the **Kashmir Valley** and the rest of India before the completion of the **Banihal-Qazigund Road Tunnel**.

questions.question: Which one of the following combinations contributes to low population density?

options.text: Harsh climate, poor soil, few roads
Flat terrain, fertile soil, urban jobs

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Harsh climate, poor soil, few roads**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Physical factors** like **Harsh climate** (extreme cold or extreme heat) significantly deter human settlement because they make living conditions uncomfortable and increase the cost of survival. Areas like the **Sahara Desert** or the **Himalayas** exhibit low density due to these climatic extremes.
 
• **Poor soil** fertility, often found in rocky terrains or areas with high acidity/alkalinity, prevents the development of **agriculture**. Since food production is the primary driver of settlement, regions with infertile soil cannot support large populations, leading to sparse habitation.
 
• **Socio-economic factors** such as **infrastructure** development play a crucial role; the presence of **few roads** indicates poor **connectivity** and isolation. Areas lacking transportation networks struggle with the delivery of essential services and trade, making them unattractive for dense population growth.
 
• The combination of these three factors creates an environment where **carrying capacity** is extremely low, meaning the land can only support a very limited number of people per **square kilometer**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Factors Contributing to High Population Density:**

 
 
• **Geographical Factors:** **River valleys** (like the **Ganges** and **Nile**) provide fresh water and **alluvial soil**, which are perfect for intensive farming.
 
• **Topographical Factors:** **Flat terrain** or plains facilitate the construction of buildings, factories, and extensive **transportation networks**.
 
• **Economic Factors:** The availability of **urban jobs**, **industrialization**, and educational institutions acts as a pull factor, attracting migrants to cities.
 
• **Social Factors:** Access to **health clinics**, **schools**, and sanitation systems improves the quality of life, leading to higher concentrations of people in urban centers.
 
 
 
• **Population Density:** Defined as the ratio between the total **population** and the total **land area**, it is a key metric in **demography** used to analyze the distribution of human life across the globe.

questions.question: Under which article can the president summon, prorogue, or dissolve either house of Parliament?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 85**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 85** of the **Indian Constitution** provides the legal framework for the sessions of **Parliament**, including their **summoning**, **prorogation**, and **dissolution**.
 
• The **President of India** is vested with the authority to **summon** each **House of Parliament** (the **Lok Sabha** and the **Rajya Sabha**) to meet at such time and place as they think fit.
 
• A mandatory constitutional requirement under **Article 85(1)** is that **six months** shall not intervene between the last sitting of one session and the date appointed for the first sitting of the next session, ensuring regular legislative functioning.
 
• Under **Article 85(2)(a)**, the **President** has the power to **prorogue** either House, which effectively ends a session of **Parliament** without dissolving the house itself.
 
• Under **Article 85(2)(b)**, the **President** possesses the power to **dissolve** the **House of the People** (**Lok Sabha**), usually on the advice of the **Council of Ministers** headed by the **Prime Minister**.
 
• It is important to note that while the **Lok Sabha** can be dissolved, the **Rajya Sabha** is a **Permanent House** and is not subject to **dissolution** as per the provisions of **Article 83**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 79**:

 
 
• This article specifies the **Constitution of Parliament**, declaring that there shall be a **Parliament** for the **Union** consisting of the **President** and two **Houses**.
 
• The two houses are the **Council of States** (**Rajya Sabha**) and the **House of the People** (**Lok Sabha**).
 
 
 
• **Article 87**:
 
 
• This pertains to the **Special Address** by the **President**.
 
• The **President** must address both Houses of **Parliament** assembled together at the commencement of the first session after each **General Election** and at the commencement of the first session of each year.
 
 
 
• **Article 108**:
 
 
• Provides for a **Joint Sitting** of both Houses in certain circumstances, such as when there is a **deadlock** over the passage of an **Ordinary Bill**.
 
• The **President** summons the **Joint Sitting**, which is presided over by the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha**.

questions.question: Which of the following is a Parliamentary committee?

options.text: A committee formed by the President
A panel of MPs selected by the House or Speaker

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A panel of MPs selected by the House or Speaker**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Parliamentary Committee** is defined under the **Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business** as a committee that is appointed or elected by the **House** (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) or nominated by the **Speaker** or the **Chairman**.
 
• The committee must consist of **Members of Parliament (MPs)** and functions under the direct authority and direction of the **Presiding Officer** of the respective House.
 
• These committees are essential because **Parliament** has a vast volume of work and limited time; hence, detailed scrutiny of legislation and executive actions is delegated to these smaller bodies.
 
• A crucial criterion for a body to be recognized as a parliamentary committee is that its **Secretariat** must be provided by the **Lok Sabha Secretariat** or the **Rajya Sabha Secretariat**.
 
• The committee presents its **reports** either to the **House** or to the **Speaker/Chairman**, ensuring accountability of the executive to the legislature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Parliamentary Committees**:

 
 
• **Standing Committees**: Permanent bodies constituted periodically (usually annually) like the **Public Accounts Committee**, **Estimates Committee**, and **Committee on Public Undertakings**.
 
• **Ad Hoc Committees**: Temporary committees appointed for a specific task, such as **Select Committees** or **Joint Committees** on specific Bills, which dissolve after submitting their report.
 
 
 
• **Financial Committees**:
 
 
• **Public Accounts Committee (PAC)**: Consists of **22 members** (15 from Lok Sabha, 7 from Rajya Sabha) and examines the reports of the **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)**.
 
• **Estimates Committee**: The largest committee with **30 members**, all exclusively from the **Lok Sabha**, focusing on efficiency in public expenditure.
 
 
 
• **Exclusions**:
 
 
• A committee formed by the **President** (like a Commission of Inquiry) is an **Executive Committee**, not a Parliamentary one.
 
• **Judicial panels** or committees of **civil servants** (departmental committees) do not fall under the legislative oversight framework of **Parliament**.

questions.question: Which strategy was used by the British to regain control after initial rebel victories across northern India in the Revolt of 1857?

options.text: Recapturing key centres, enacting new laws, and offering rewards to loyal chiefs.
Negotiating a settlement that restored regional rulers to their former positions.
Withdrawing British forces from major towns to avoid further confrontation.
Allowing the Mughal emperor to govern Delhi under strict British supervision.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Recapturing key centres, enacting new laws, and offering rewards to loyal chiefs.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Military Reinforcements and Recapture:** To suppress the **Revolt of 1857**, the British government brought military reinforcements from **England**. They launched a focused offensive on major rebel hubs, successfully recapturing **Delhi** in **September 1857**. The **Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar** was subsequently captured, tried, and exiled to **Rangoon**.
 
• **Legislative Crackdown:** The British enacted **new laws** designed to bypass standard judicial procedures. These laws empowered military officers and administrators to conduct **summary trials**, making it significantly easier to convict and execute suspected rebels and their sympathizers.
 
• **Incentivizing Loyalty:** Recognizing the influence of local elites, the British announced **rewards** and **guarantees** for **loyal landholders** (Zamindars). They were assured that if they had not participated in the killing of British officials, they would be allowed to retain their **traditional rights** over their lands and estates.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fall of Major Resistance Hubs:**

 
 
• **Lucknow** was recaptured by the British in **March 1858**, effectively breaking the rebel hold in **Awadh**.
 
• **Jhansi** fell in **June 1858** following the defeat and death of **Rani Lakshmibai**, who had become a symbol of resistance.
 
 
 
• **End of Company Rule:** The failure of the **East India Company** to prevent the uprising led to the **Government of India Act 1858**, which transferred administrative power directly to the **British Crown**.
 
• **Shift in Annexation Policy:** To prevent future mutinies among Indian royals, the British abandoned the **Doctrine of Lapse** and issued a **Proclamation** ensuring that Indian states would no longer be annexed, provided they accepted the **Queen of England** as their **Sovereign Paramount**.

questions.question: Which of the following explains that during a chemical reaction, the sum of masses of the reactants and products remains unchanged?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Law of Conservation of Mass**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Law of Conservation of Mass** states that mass in an isolated system is neither **created** nor **destroyed** by chemical reactions or physical transformations.
 
• According to this law, the **total mass of the reactants** must be equal to the **total mass of the products** in a chemical reaction.
 
• The French chemist **Antoine Lavoisier** formulated this principle in **1789**, which is why he is often referred to as the **Father of Modern Chemistry**.
 
• At a molecular level, this occurs because atoms are merely **rearranged** during a chemical reaction; the total number of atoms of each element remains constant, thus preserving the overall mass.
 
• For example, in the combustion of **methane**, the sum of the masses of methane and oxygen consumed will exactly equal the sum of the masses of **carbon dioxide** and **water vapor** produced.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Law of Definite Proportions** (also known as **Law of Definite Composition**):

 
 
• Proposed by **Joseph Proust** in **1799**.
 
• It states that a **chemical compound** always contains its component elements in a **fixed ratio** by mass, regardless of the source or method of preparation.
 
• For instance, **pure water** will always contain **88.8%** oxygen and **11.2%** hydrogen by mass.
 
 
 
• **Law of Periodicity**:
 
 
• Refers to the recurring variation in **element properties** with increasing **atomic number**.
 
• This principle is the basis of the **Modern Periodic Table**, where elements with similar chemical behaviors are placed in the same **vertical groups**.
